rewritten_text:
“Tom!”

No reply.

“TOM!”

No reply.

“Where on earth has that boy gone? TOM, you hear me?”

No reply.

The old woman lowered her glasses and surveyed the room over them, then pushed them up and peered underneath. She rarely, if ever, looked through them for anything as insignificant as a boy. They were her best pair, her pride and joy, made for appearance rather than use; she could have seen just as well through two iron stove lids. Looking puzzled for a moment, she then said, without real ferocity but loudly enough for the furniture to hear:

“Well, if I get my hands on you, I'll—”

She broke off, because she was now bending over and jabbing beneath the bed with a broom, and needed her breath to accompany the jabs. All she brought to light was the cat.

“I've never known a boy like him!”

She went to the open doorway, stood there, and searched the tomato plants and jimson weeds that made up the garden. No Tom. So she raised her voice, aiming it to carry as far as possible, and shouted:

“Y-o-o-u, TOM!”

A faint sound came from behind her. She turned just in time to catch a small boy by the loose fabric of his short jacket and stop his escape.

“There! I should have thought of that closet. What were you doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. Look at your mouth. What is that stuff?”

“I don't know, Aunt.”

“Well, I do. It's jam, that's what. I've told you forty times I'd give you a hiding if you didn't leave that jam alone. Hand me that switch.”

The switch hung in the air. His danger was desperate.

“Oh! Look behind you, Aunt!”

The old woman spun around and snatched her skirts away from danger. Instantly the boy bolted, scrambled up the tall wooden fence, and vanished over it.

Aunt Polly stood astonished for a moment, then began to laugh softly.

“Confound that boy, will I never learn? Hasn't he pulled enough tricks like that for me to be on my guard by now? But old fools are the worst fools of all. You can't teach an old dog new tricks, as they say. Still, goodness knows, he never does the same thing two days running. How can anyone know what to expect? He seems to know exactly how long he can torment me before I lose my temper, and he knows that if he can distract me for a minute, or make me laugh, my anger disappears and I can't bring myself to hit him.”

“What's wrong?”

“It's ten o'clock, sir.”

“What do you mean? Ten at night?”

“Yes, sir. You asked me to wake you.”

“Oh, I remember. All right, all right.”

He made a few sleepy attempts to drift off again, but the man cleverly prevented this by poking the fire without stopping for five minutes. At last he got up, threw on his hat, and went out. He entered the Temple, walked twice along the pavements of King's Bench Walk and Paper Buildings to wake himself properly, and then went to Stryver's chambers.

Stryver's clerk, who never took part in these meetings, had gone home, so Stryver himself opened the door. He wore slippers and a loose dressing gown, with his neck uncovered for comfort. Around his eyes was that wild, strained, scorched look common to hard-drinking men of his kind. It appears in the portrait of Jeffries and, beneath the various styles painters use, in portraits from every age of heavy drinking.

“You're a little late, Memory,” Stryver said.

“About the usual time. Perhaps fifteen minutes later.”

They entered a gloomy room lined with books and covered in papers, where a strong fire burned. A kettle steamed beside it. Among the scattered papers stood a gleaming table, well supplied with wine, brandy, rum, sugar and lemons.

“I see you've had your bottle, Sydney.”

“Two tonight, I think. I've been dining with today's client—or watching him dine. It amounts to the same thing!”

“That was an excellent point you made about the identification, Sydney. How did you think of it? When did it occur to you?”

“I thought he was a rather handsome fellow, and that I might have been much the same myself if I'd had any luck.”

Mr. Stryver laughed until his already developing belly shook.

“You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work, get to work.”

Looking thoroughly sulky, the jackal loosened his clothes and went into the next room. He returned with a large jug of cold water, a basin and a towel or two. He soaked the towels, partly wrung them out, and folded them over his head, making a dreadful sight. Then he sat at the table and announced, “Now I'm ready!”

“Not much to sort through and boil down tonight, Memory,” Mr. Stryver said cheerfully, looking through his papers.

“How much?”

“Only two sets.”

“Give me the worst first.”

“There you are, Sydney. Get started!”

The lion then settled on his back on a sofa beside the drinks table. The jackal sat at his own paper-covered worktable on the opposite side, with the bottles and glasses close at hand.

I come from a little corner ringed by sea, a country beneath the shadow of clouds, which, when I picture the globe with its boundless ocean and uncharted continents, seems but a trifling dot in that enormous whole; yet measured by intellectual strength, it greatly surpassed lands of wider territory and more abundant inhabitants. Thus truly did the mind of man alone create whatever was good or great for him, while Nature served only as his chief minister. England, lying far to the north amid the troubled waters, appears in my dreams now as a mighty ship, amply manned, commanding the winds and riding the waves in pride. In childhood she constituted my universe. Standing upon the hills of my birthplace, watching mountains and plains extend to the furthest edge of sight, dotted with my countrymen's homes and rendered fruitful by their toil, I placed the very centre of the earth upon that spot. The remainder of its sphere seemed a mere story, which neither my understanding nor my fancy would have found any difficulty in forgetting.

From their outset my fortunes have illustrated the sway of change over the diverse course of human existence. In my case this was almost an inheritance. My father belonged to those men upon whom nature lavishes the coveted powers of wit and imagination, then abandons their vessel of life to those driving winds, supplying neither reason for a rudder nor judgment to pilot the voyage. He came of obscure parentage, but circumstances soon brought him before the public, and the modest estate inherited from his father quickly vanished in the brilliant world of luxury and fashion where he played his part. Throughout the brief years of careless youth, fashionable idlers worshipped him, not least the young sovereign, who fled party intrigue and the burdens of royal duty to find unfailing entertainment and refreshment in his company. My father's impulses, which he never governed, constantly involved him in embarrassments from which only his ingenuity could rescue him. The rising heap of debts, both to tradesmen and of honour, would have crushed another man; he bore it with buoyant spirits and irrepressible merriment. Meanwhile his presence was so indispensable at the dinners and gatherings of the wealthy that his faults were treated as slight offences, and he was welcomed with flattery that intoxicated him.

Popularity of this sort, like every sort, soon passes. The difficulties of all kinds that confronted him multiplied at an alarming rate beside the scant resources he possessed for escaping them.
